newsitem.title: USA: Fed must stay ahead of inflation curve -- Broaddus.
newsitem.headline: Fed must stay ahead of inflation curve -- Broaddus.

text.p: Richmond Federal Reserve Bank President Alfred Broaddus said on Thursday that it was important the Fed stay ahead of the inflation curve.
Broaddus was speaking to a local audience of bankers and Richmond Federal Reserve officials.

The Richmond Fed president said the best time to attack inflation was precisely when inflation pressures in the economy were lacking. As a result, he said central bank monetary policy should be preemptive.

"The time to fight inflation is precisely when there isn't much inflation," Broaddus said. "It's important for the nation's economic welfare that we stay ahead of the inflation curve in conducting policy."
Broaddus said the economy has not yet registered substantial increases in wages and prices.
"We have not yet seen significant increases in wages and prices," Broaddus said. "At least not as significant as you might expect with such tight labor markets," he added.

Broaddus said such a phenomenon was the result of two main factors: a rise in productivity and increased competition in several markets. More intense competition came primarily from the international scene in the context of a stronger dollar.
He said business conditions were strong, adding that between 1995 and 1997 activity picked up.
"So far as we can tell about '97 ... the higher level of activity has been maintained in the first quarter, which we just completed, and maybe even strengthened a bit," he said.
"Basically what we see is ... stronger general demand for business and services. Consumer spending propelled a strong growth in jobs," Broaddus added.

The Richmond Fed chief said Fed monetary policy was trying to promote the continuation of a sustainable growth scenario. He added, however, that the growth rate recently seen was not likely to be sustained without an uptick in inflation.

"There is absolutely nothing wrong with growth. The economy is supposed to grow and that's what policy is trying to promote ... (but) the kind of growth we seem to be seeing over the last six months is probably not sustainable without at some point giving rise to some increase in inflationary pressures, given the longer-term growth in the nation's labor force and productivity," Broaddus said.
Citing a consensus estimate of professional forecasters, Broaddus said economic activity was expected to slow somewhat in 1997.

"Real GDP (Gross Domestic Product) ... is expected to diminish in '97 to a little under a 3.0 percent rate for the year, following a growth of all of 1996 of a little over 3.0 percent. That's a little slower growth but still quite robust economic growth," the Richmond Fed president said.
Broaddus also said forecasts indicate the U.S. might see a rise in inflation in 1997. "We might expect a little bit of an uptick to someting like 3.0 percent."

As for the housing market, Broaddus said, "Housing activity across the country -- and of course there will be a lot of variations across the country -- but generally it's expected to be a reasonably good year, perhaps not quite as robust as last year, especially since mortgage rates have moved up, but in any event still a reaonably good year."
